title: Stroke Rehabilitation
shortDescription: Therapy and guidance to help recovery of movement, function and independence after a stroke.
introduction: After a stroke, many people have difficulties with movement, balance, speech, thinking or daily activities. Recovery is often greatest in the weeks and months after a stroke, but improvement can continue for longer.
Stroke rehabilitation uses targeted exercises and practical training to help people regain abilities, adapt to changes and reduce the risk of complications such as stiffness and falls.
symptomsOrReasons: Weakness or stiffness of an arm or leg after a stroke
Difficulty walking, standing or keeping your balance
Problems using your hand for daily tasks
Reduced confidence or fear of falling
Caregivers needing guidance on how to give safe support at home
whatToExpect: An assessment of movement, strength, balance and daily activities.
Setting practical goals with you and your family.
Exercises and activity training adapted to your needs.
A home exercise plan and regular review of progress.
whoMayBenefit: People recovering from a recent stroke
People with longer-standing difficulties after a stroke who want to improve function
Families and caregivers supporting stroke recovery
preparation: Any walking aids, splints or braces you use
Your hospital discharge summary and any previous therapy notes
nextSteps: Your plan is adjusted as you progress.
You may be given exercises to continue at home between sessions.

faqs.question: When should stroke rehabilitation start?
faqs.answer: Rehabilitation usually starts once the person is medically stable. The doctor will advise on timing for your situation.

faqs.question: Can improvement continue months after a stroke?
faqs.answer: Yes. Many people continue to make gains with ongoing practice and therapy, although progress differs from person to person.

title: Parkinson's Rehabilitation
shortDescription: Exercise and therapy to support movement, balance and daily activities in Parkinson's disease.
introduction: Parkinson's disease can cause slowness, stiffness, tremor and balance problems. Alongside medicines, regular exercise and therapy play an important role in staying active and independent.
Parkinson's rehabilitation focuses on walking, balance, flexibility, posture and practical strategies for everyday tasks.
symptomsOrReasons: Slowness or stiffness affecting daily activities
Shuffling steps, freezing or difficulty turning
Balance problems or falls
A stooped posture
Wanting a safe and regular exercise routine
whatToExpect: An assessment of movement, walking, balance and posture.
Exercises for strength, flexibility and balance.
Strategies for walking, turning and getting up from a chair.
Advice on staying active at home.
whoMayBenefit: People with Parkinson's disease at any stage
People with other movement disorders affecting walking or balance
Caregivers who want to support exercise safely
preparation: A list of your medicines and the times you usually take them
nextSteps: Your exercise plan is adjusted as your needs change.
A home exercise routine may be suggested to help you stay active.

faqs.question: Can exercise help in Parkinson's disease?
faqs.answer: Regular, appropriate exercise can help with mobility, balance and wellbeing. A therapist can suggest exercises that are safe for you.

faqs.question: Will rehabilitation replace my medicines?
faqs.answer: No. Rehabilitation works alongside the treatment advised by your doctor.

title: Neuromuscular Rehabilitation
shortDescription: Therapy to maintain strength, mobility and function in nerve and muscle conditions.
introduction: Nerve and muscle conditions, such as neuropathy, myopathy and Guillain-Barré syndrome, can cause weakness, numbness, tiredness and balance problems.
Neuromuscular rehabilitation aims to maintain and improve strength and mobility, protect joints, manage fatigue and support independence, with exercise matched to the condition.
symptomsOrReasons: Weakness in the arms or legs
Balance problems caused by numbness in the feet
Tiredness that limits daily activities
Recovery after an episode of Guillain-Barré syndrome
Needing advice on walking aids or splints
whatToExpect: An assessment of strength, sensation, balance and stamina.
A tailored exercise programme that avoids overworking weak muscles.
Advice on saving energy and staying safe.
whoMayBenefit: People with neuropathy, myopathy or other neuromuscular conditions
preparation: Any splints, braces or walking aids you use
nextSteps: Your programme is reviewed and adjusted as your strength and needs change.
Home exercises may be provided to continue between sessions.

faqs.question: Is exercise safe with a muscle condition?
faqs.answer: Appropriate exercise is often helpful, but the type and intensity need to suit your condition. Your programme will be planned with this in mind.

faqs.question: Can therapy help with numb feet?
faqs.answer: Balance training and foot-care advice can help reduce falls and protect the feet when feeling is reduced.

title: Physiotherapy
shortDescription: Exercise-based treatment to improve movement, strength, balance and pain.
introduction: Physiotherapy uses exercise, movement training and other physical techniques to help people move better, reduce pain and recover function.
For neurological conditions, physiotherapy often focuses on strength, balance, walking, posture and preventing stiffness.
symptomsOrReasons: Weakness or stiffness after a stroke or another neurological condition
Back or neck pain, including pain with sciatica
Balance problems or a risk of falls
Reduced mobility or difficulty walking
whatToExpect: An assessment of movement, strength and pain.
A personalised treatment plan with clear goals.
Guided exercises during sessions.
Exercises to continue at home.
whoMayBenefit: People with back, neck or nerve pain
People with balance or walking difficulties
preparation: Previous reports or a note from your doctor, if available
nextSteps: Your progress is reviewed regularly and the plan updated.
You will be shown exercises to continue at home.

faqs.question: How many sessions will I need?
faqs.answer: It depends on your condition and goals. Your progress will be reviewed regularly.

faqs.question: Should exercises be painful?
faqs.answer: Some effort and mild discomfort can be expected, but tell the therapist if any exercise causes significant pain.

title: Balance & Gait Training
shortDescription: Exercises to improve steadiness and walking, build confidence and reduce the risk of falls.
introduction: Balance and walking (gait) can be affected by many neurological conditions, by inner-ear problems, or by weakness or numbness in the legs and feet.
Balance and gait training uses graded exercises and walking practice to improve steadiness, build confidence and lower the risk of falls.
symptomsOrReasons: Unsteadiness or dizziness when walking
Falls or near-falls
Shuffling or uneven walking
Fear of falling that limits your activity
Using a walking aid and wanting to walk more safely
whatToExpect: An assessment of standing balance, walking pattern and fall risk.
Exercises for balance, strength and coordination.
Advice on walking aids and on safety at home.
whoMayBenefit: People with balance problems due to neurological or inner-ear conditions
Older adults at risk of falls
People recovering from stroke or living with Parkinson's disease
preparation: Any walking aid you currently use
nextSteps: Exercises are progressed as your balance improves.
A home programme may be suggested to keep practising safely.

faqs.question: Can balance improve with exercise?
faqs.answer: For many people, regular targeted practice improves balance and confidence. Results vary depending on the cause.

faqs.question: How can I reduce the risk of falls at home?
faqs.answer: Good lighting, removing loose rugs, using handrails and wearing supportive footwear can help. The therapist can give advice specific to your home.

title: Cognitive Rehabilitation
shortDescription: Strategies and exercises to help with memory, attention and thinking difficulties.
introduction: Cognitive rehabilitation helps people manage difficulties with memory, attention, planning and problem-solving after a stroke, brain injury or other neurological condition.
It focuses on practical strategies, such as routines, memory aids and step-by-step planning, along with exercises that make everyday tasks easier.
symptomsOrReasons: Forgetfulness that affects daily life
Difficulty concentrating or following conversations
Trouble planning or organising tasks
Thinking difficulties after a stroke or brain injury
whatToExpect: An assessment of the specific thinking difficulties and the daily challenges they cause.
Setting goals that matter to you.
Practising strategies and using aids such as diaries, reminders and checklists.
Involving family members where this helps.
whoMayBenefit: People with thinking difficulties after a stroke or brain injury
People with mild memory problems who want practical strategies
Families supporting a person with memory difficulties
preparation: Results of any previous cognitive or neuropsychological assessments
If possible, a family member who can help with practising strategies at home
nextSteps: Strategies are reviewed and adapted to your progress.
Practical tools may be suggested for use at home and work.

faqs.question: Can cognitive rehabilitation cure memory loss?
faqs.answer: It cannot reverse every cause of memory loss, but it can help people cope better and stay more independent.

faqs.question: Is it useful for people with dementia?
faqs.answer: Strategies and routines can help some people with early dementia manage daily life. The doctor will advise whether it is suitable.

title: Home Exercise Guidance
shortDescription: Safe, practical exercise plans to continue your recovery at home.
introduction: Regular practice between therapy sessions is an important part of recovery for many neurological conditions.
Home exercise guidance provides a simple, safe programme tailored to your abilities, with clear instructions for you and your caregivers.
symptomsOrReasons: Continuing progress between or after therapy sessions
Difficulty travelling for frequent sessions
Needing a safe routine to stay active
Caregivers wanting to help with exercises
whatToExpect: A review of your current abilities and your home situation.
A demonstration of exercises you can do safely.
Written or illustrated instructions to follow.
Follow-up to update the programme.
whoMayBenefit: People receiving rehabilitation who want to keep practising at home
preparation: Notes about your home, such as stairs, space and handrails, that may affect which exercises are safe
nextSteps: Your home programme is updated as you progress.
Contact the clinic if an exercise causes pain or difficulty.

faqs.question: How often should I do my home exercises?
faqs.answer: Follow the frequency advised in your programme. Regular, consistent practice is usually more helpful than occasional long sessions.

faqs.question: What if an exercise causes pain or dizziness?
faqs.answer: Stop the exercise and contact the clinic for advice. Seek urgent medical help for any emergency symptoms.
